sections.changelog:
Added

  • **The model number in a query is mandatory (*Relevance → Model number is mandatory*, on by default).** A word carrying a digit is the one thing that separates two otherwise identical parts, and the strictness floor treated it as one optional concept among many: "iphone 16 pro max lcd" cleared the floor on its other four words, so iPhone 13 and 15 screens came back alongside the 16. Worse, a glued code arrived as a bag of alternatives — "note13" expands to note13 / note / 13, any one of which satisfied the group — so a Redmi Note 8 counted as a full match. Measured on a 13k-product catalogue: "note13" returned 1000 rows of which 89 were a Note 13, "8s" returned 1000 of which 23 were an 8S, "стекло samsung a51" returned 1000 of which a third were an M51. A glued code is now resolved against the catalogue first — asking whether any term starts with it, which also reaches "g980f" from "g980" — and only when nothing carries it whole does it fall back to its parts, all of which are then required. On a catalogue rebuilt to the same shape the five measured queries went from 10–55% on-target to 100%, and the cost is one indexed prefix lookup per model word: 0.3–0.7 ms against an index of 270k rows, cached for ten minutes. Required groups are also left out of the typo pass — model numbers sit one edit apart ("16" and "15", "a51" and "a52"), so a fuzzy variant there would quietly answer with the neighbouring part. The word under the cursor is exempt while the dropdown is being typed into: a half-written number is a keystroke, not a requirement, and demanding it turned "iphone 1" into a hunt for the digit 1 — the phones the shopper was reaching for gave way to unrelated products whose names happen to carry a 1. A model nobody carries at all still answers rather than dead-ending: the ladder's final attempt drops the requirement. Turn the setting off for catalogues where a neighbouring model is a welcome suggestion.

Fixed

  • **A supplier's article number no longer seeds the index with model numbers.** Any token holding a digit is split into its letter and digit runs so a glued code stays searchable by any part ("gtx1660" → gtx + 1660). Applied to a machine identifier that produces nonsense: the SKU `683ec6c16ede0cd1bc9bbc5d` came apart into twelve terms — `683`, `ec`, `6`, `16`, `ede`, `0`, `cd`, `1`, `bc`, `9`, `bbc`, `5` — and every digit run among them landed in the index with the weight of an article number, where it reads exactly like a model. On the measured catalogue 109 products carried a bogus `16` that way, 260 a bogus `13`, and a search for one article number returned 50 products instead of one. Identifier fields (SKU, variation SKU, GTIN) are now split only while the token stays within a run budget, and the same budget applies to the query side so a pasted article number is not torn apart either. Real codes are unaffected — measured on the same catalogue, 13 096 of 13 129 supplier SKUs exceed the budget against 275 of 19 984 title tokens. Article numbers are still indexed whole, so an exact lookup works as before; reindex to clear the fragments already stored.
  • **Two queries with the same terms but a different word structure no longer share an expansion.** The coverage-group cache keyed on the flat term list, which loses the word boundaries: "ф515" (one word yielding `ф515` and `515`) and "ф515 515" (two words yielding the same two terms) hashed to the same key, so whichever ran first handed its grouping to the other — one concept where there should be two, or the reverse, which moves the strictness floor. Rare before; the model handling above makes it routine, since a glued code is now split into separate words. The key keeps the boundaries.
  • **A search that finds nothing steps down instead of falling open.** The zero-result retry dropped the floor straight to 1 — an OR across every word — so the strict setting was the noisiest of the three whenever one query word matched nothing at all: on the measured catalogue "iPhone 16 po max lcd" returned 500 rows, 294 without a 16 anywhere, because the mistyped "po" is too short for a fuzzy variant and made the AND pass empty. The floor now descends one rung at a time and stops at the first rung that answers.
  • **Lowering the article-number field weight no longer looks like a relevance control.** Not a code change, but worth stating: coverage is counted without weights, so the weight only orders what already matched. Measured at 10, 5, 1 and 0, the result set and the positions of every off-target row were identical; at 1 and below the product's own article number stopped finding it at all. The fix for article-number noise is the indexing change above.
  • **Appearance settings for the search bar reach the field on any theme.** The border colour, field background and text colour were set on the plugin's own classes, and a theme styling `input[type="search"]` outweighs a single class — so those three settings did nothing while the button and its magnifier, whose classes no theme knows, worked fine. Measured on the test stand: `#ff0000` requested, `rgb(206,212,218)` rendered. Two changes: the rules that style the native elements now carry the form's class as well, and a colour the admin actually chose is stated once more with `!important`. Raising specificity alone was not enough — measured across ten popular themes, nine were covered by the class pair and Twenty Twenty-One still won the button with `button:not(:hover):not(:active):not(.has-background)`, which no reasonable class chain outweighs. Only settings that carry a value are restated, so an untouched setting still leaves the theme in charge; and the restated value is read back through the custom property, so a theme that customises the bar by redefining `--mvweb-ss-*` keeps its colours. A theme that wants the whole bar to itself can drop these rules with the new `mvweb_ss_force_appearance` filter.
  • **The magnifier inside the field follows the icon colour.** It is drawn as a background image, and an image cannot read a CSS variable for its stroke, so the setting only ever reached the bare icon of the collapsed display mode and left the in-field one grey. The whole image is now rebuilt with the chosen colour. Left unset, the icon stays as it was, so no site changes appearance on update. The field hint now names both places the setting applies to, and points at the separate colour for the magnifier on the button.
